name: Bodiman
overview: A small Sawa people of the banks of the Wouri, the Bodiman live among the Ewodi, Duala, Banen and Basaa of Yabassi, whose languages they speak. Having come from Congo, fishers and farmers, they have the canoe, the paddle and the crocodile as symbols, and every December celebrate the Suunɛm Ebanabamboa, which has become the festival of the Bodiman canton.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Minority group, integrated with the Ewodi, Duala, Banen and Basaa of Yabassi; many speak Basaa, Wodi and Duala.
Mixed group, open to marriages with other peoples, especially on the men's side.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: The Bodiman look after their ancestral land, reputed to be fertile.
Its symbols are the dugout canoe, the paddle and the crocodile.
A people on the move who came from Congo, it has kept no ties with its places of origin.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: A king of the community, third-degree chiefdoms, village and canton chiefs; decisions are made at the chiefdom, by consensus.
Relations are free; respect remains the basis of every family.
Succession goes from father to son.
The mangond, women dignitaries, sang during rituals, advised on the appointment of village chiefs and could hold back the rain during an event; they also acted as priestesses and oracles.
Ancestral alliance relations with the neighbours.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the wife goes to live with her husband.
The boy becomes a man through circumcision, then by leaving the parental home; the girl becomes a woman by marrying. People marry at around 25 for men, 18 for women.
Steps: “knocking at the door”, marriage proposal, bride price.
Bride price: suit for the father, kaba for the mother, dried cod, salt, red wine, goat, whisky; these gifts seal the union and mark the young woman's separation from her family.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: The ŋgambi, a night cult led by a great initiate, used to be held in caves; there are others.
Sacred places: the water, the barrier of baobabs (kɔrɔmabuma), the confluence of the Nnam and the Wouri (Dibowɛ).
Birth is a reincarnation or a natural fact; death, a natural phenomenon. The bond with the dead is never broken: they are visited every year.
Incest is taboo.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: fishing, farming, trap hunting. Women: fishing, farming, home.
The land belongs to the extended family.
Few crafts: raffia palm mats for the house.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Wrapper and shirt for men, kaba ŋgondo for women.
Traditional medicine remains highly prized for certain illnesses.
Beauty: the robust, tall, strong man, a good fisherman and good dancer; the woman of good conduct, hard-working, exemplary, welcoming and helpful.
Courtship: good fisherman and sweet talker; the woman with a melodious voice (ŋgoso).

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms: ésɛwɛ, ambassibé, bolobo, makossa; instruments: mukeŋ drum, tam-tam, Chinese bamboo.
Dances: ésɛwɛ at the wake of a patriarch, bolobo at sunset, bele at weddings.
Festival: the Suunɛm Ebanabamboa, every December, now the festival of the Bodiman canton.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: The Bodiman way of life is very close to those of the Duala and the Basaa.

sections.title: The names
items: No naming procedure: the name depends on circumstances; it is rarely changed (an unacknowledged child, for example).
Terms of address: mola (uncle), tanty (aunt), ata or tare (dad), yu, nolo, elo; appellative à-: à-Mfɔmu, à-Ŋgalɛ.

lessons.title: Who are the Bodiman? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Bodiman community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Bodiman community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Bodiman community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Bodiman community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Bodiman community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Bodiman call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Minority group, integrated with the Ewodi, Duala, Banen and Basaa of Yabassi; many speak Basaa, Wodi and Duala. • Mixed group, open to marriages with other peoples, especially on the men's side. • The Bodiman look after their ancestral land, reputed to be fertile. • Its symbols are the dugout canoe, the paddle and the crocodile.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: A small Sawa people of the banks of the Wouri, the Bodiman live among the Ewodi, Duala, Banen and Basaa of Yabassi, whose languages they speak. Having come from Congo, fishers and farmers, they have the canoe, the paddle and the crocodile as symbols, and every December celebrate the Suunɛm Ebanabamboa, which has become the festival of the Bodiman canton.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Bodiman community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Bodiman
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
lessons.competence: Describe how the Bodiman organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision must be made for the whole Bodiman village. Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe how the Bodiman organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “An important decision has to be made for the whole Bodiman village. Who decides, and how?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • A king of the community, 3rd-degree chiefdoms, village and canton chiefs; decisions are made at the chiefdom, by consensus. • Relations are free; respect remains the basis of every family. • Succession passes from father to son. • The mangond, women dignitaries, sang during rituals, advised on the appointment of village chiefs and could hold back the rain during an event; they also acted as priestesses and oracles. • Ancestral alliance relations with the neighbours.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: A king of the community, third-degree chiefdoms, village and canton chiefs; decisions are made at the chiefdom, by consensus. Relations are free; respect remains the basis of every family. Succession is from father to son.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a diagram (organisation chart) of power among the Bodiman, then explain in 3 sentences how a decision is made.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Bodiman
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Bodiman, describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Bodiman.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Bodiman, describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Bodiman.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: sweet potato and yam, fish, aubergines. • Drinks: arki, palm wine. • Men: fishing, farming, trap hunting. Women: fishing, farming, home. • The land belongs to the extended family.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Bodiman mainly eat potato and yam, fish, aubergines. Traditional drinks: arki, palm wine. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Bodiman: write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Birth, name and the passage to adulthood among the Bodiman
objectives: Explain the meaning of a birth
lessons.competence: Explain how the Bodiman welcome a child, give the child a name and mark the child's entry into adulthood.
lessons.situation: A child has just been born in a Bodiman family. How will he be named, and how will he become an adult?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain how the Bodiman welcome a child, give it a name and mark its entry into adulthood.

steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A child has just been born in a Bodiman family. How will they be named, and how will they become an adult?” The students think individually.

steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

The bond with the dead is never broken: they are visited every year. • The boy becomes a man through circumcision, then by leaving the parental home; the girl becomes a woman by marrying. People marry around 25 for men, 18 for women.

lessons.title: Marriage and bride price among the Bodiman

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)

lessons.title: Leisure: traditional music and dances of the Bodiman
objectives: Describe a dance and its instruments
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Bodiman, choose the most representative one, describe it, bring out its cultural significance and act it out.

lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Bodiman
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Bodiman, the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Bodiman. First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Bodiman, the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Bodiman. First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Men: fishing, farming, trap hunting. Women: fishing, farming, home. • Land belongs to the extended family. • Few crafts: raffia palm mats for the house.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: fishing, farming, trap hunting. Women: fishing, farming, home. Land belongs to the extended family.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Bodiman's activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover how the Bodiman make a living from their work.

activities.title: I classify
activities.instruction: Classify the activities in a men / women table.

activities.title: I explain
activities.instruction: Explain how one obtains land to cultivate.

activities.title: I calculate
activities.instruction: Imagine the calendar of a working year (seasons, harvests, festivals).

activities.title: I propose
activities.instruction: Suggest a project idea that promotes a local skill.

student.memo: Men: fishing, farming, trap hunting. Women: fishing, farming, home. Land belongs to the extended family.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Bodiman
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death

vocabulary.frenchText: confluence of the Nnam and Wouri

lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Bodiman, and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Bodiman. Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Bodiman, and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Bodiman. Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The ŋgambi, a night cult led by a great initiate, used to be held in caves; there are others. • Sacred places: water, the barrier of baobabs (kɔrɔmabuma), the confluence of the Nnam and the Wouri (Dibowɛ). • Birth is a reincarnation or a natural event; death, a natural phenomenon. The bond with the dead is never broken: they are visited every year. • Incest is taboo.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The ŋgambi, a night cult led by a great initiate, used to be held in caves; there are others. Sacred places: water, the baobab barrier (kɔrɔmabuma), the confluence of the Nnam and the Wouri (Dibowɛ).

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Bodiman (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover what the Bodiman believe, the places they respect and the taboos they observe.

activities.title: I identify
activities.instruction: Identify two sacred places and what they recall.

activities.title: I explain
activities.instruction: Explain the usefulness of a taboo for the life of the group.

activities.title: I show respect
activities.instruction: Write the guide for the respectful visitor.

activities.title: I compare
activities.instruction: Compare with a taboo you know in your family.

student.memo: The ŋgambi, a night cult led by a great initiate, used to be held in caves; there are others. Sacred places: water, the baobab barrier (kɔrɔmabuma), the confluence of the Nnam and the Wouri (Dibowɛ).

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Bodiman
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Bodiman and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Bodiman family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Bodiman greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Bodiman family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The community's language is Bodiman. • Greetings: “Ma᷅so᷇ma᷅” = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); “mɔɔni” = morning greeting (one person); “masomnɔ” = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Fɔ᷇, Beɓa᷅a᷇, belaalo, Binyi᷅i᷇, Bitan᷅. • Terms of address: mola (uncle), tanty (aunt), ata or tare (dad), yu, nolo, elo; the à- form of address: à-Mfɔmu, à-Ŋgalɛ. • The Bodiman way of life is very close to those of the Duala and the Basaa.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Bodiman are the first steps towards communicating with the Bodiman. Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Bodiman.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Bodiman are the first steps towards communicating with the Bodiman. Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
